prompt:
Use case: ui-mockup.
Create a single convincing GAMEPLAY SCREENSHOT of an original top-down 2D Game Boy Color-style adventure, working title LOW TIDE, for kids ages 9–12. This is deliberately very simple, flat, chunky pixel art, like an actual late-1990s cartridge game. NOT modern HD pixel art, NOT an isometric game, NOT painterly, NOT a 3D scene, NOT cinematic concept art. No handheld hardware frame or big advertising title.
Image composition: a nearly square 10:9 game screen, inspired by a 160x144 logical pixel resolution shown at a crisp integer enlargement. Everything uses visible large square pixels, hard nearest-neighbor edges, a consistent small tile grid, simple repeating textures, and compact 16-pixel-style character sprites. Limited Game Boy Color palette: warm sand, ochre, muted teal, navy outline, terracotta roofs, a few sea-green accents. Maximum four colors in each individual tile or sprite where practical. No gradients, no bloom, no soft shadows, no realistic water reflections, no tiny high-resolution detail. Camera is flat orthographic overhead with only simple front faces of buildings, matching classic top-down Game Boy Color maps. No horizon, no perspective convergence, no diamond grid.
STORY MOMENT: The bay has mysteriously drained overnight and your older brother Finn has not come home. The playable child in a red jacket and dark hair has just found Finn's blue wooden boat stranded on the sandy harbor floor, with his yellow scarf caught on its bow. A narrow trail of chalk arrows points from the boat toward an old wreck and a dark passage in the harbor wall. This is a mystery exploration game, not a score game.
WORLD LAYOUT: a small harbor town along the upper edge with two very simple orange-roofed houses and a teal-roofed bait shop; compact wooden dock extending down from upper left over exposed sand; a very small old lighthouse at upper right, at exactly the same map scale as houses. The lower and middle screen are the exposed sandy seabed, with the stranded blue boat central-right, shells, two puddles made from flat blue tiles, and one crab sprite. Child player sprite stands to the left of the boat examining scarf. A broken plank and a crate form a readable little traversal puzzle near lower-left; the path across the harbor is clear. A dark square doorway through the seawall upper-middle is barred by a piece of driftwood. No crowds, no giant characters, no party creatures, no battle interface.
UI: a tiny strip at top has exactly three red heart icons on left and one rope-hook inventory icon on right. No minimap, no score, no currencies, no quest tracker. Bottom of game screen a classic navy-outlined cream dialogue box, simple big bitmap font, text exactly two lines:
"Finn's boat..."
"Where did he go?"
The player and scenery remain visible above the dialogue box. Keep text crisp, visibly pixelated and readable, with no additional captions. The game should look implementable as a modest flat tile-map adventure with a story, exploration, conversations and a single versatile rope-hook tool. Strict retro GBC simplicity is essential; prefer sparse authentic cartridge graphics over intricate modern pixel illustration.
